title: Taiwan’s Local Elections Are Not About China, President Lai, or the United States
author: Lev Nachman
text:
Legislator and New Taipei City mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui and New Taipei City councilor Chang Chin-hao at the opening of their joint campaign headquarters in Xizhi District, New Taipei, Taiwan, Sep. 28, 2026.
Credit: Facebook/Su Chiao-hui
This November, Taiwanese voters go to the polls to elect mayors, city councilors, and village chiefs. Many foreign policy observers will read the results as a verdict on Taiwanese attitudes toward China, President Lai Ching-te, Trump, or a potential war. That would be an analytical mistake. The outcomes cannot be explained by how voters feel about independence, unification, China, the United States, or any other national issue. As the saying goes, local elections are about local issues.Decades of data show that Taiwanese voters prioritize China, sovereignty, and Taiwan’s future in national elections, but we have little longitudinal data on how they decide in local ones. What we do know is that voters often cast ballots for mayor or city council differently than they do for president. For example, Taichung and New Taipei have elected a Kuomintang (KMT) mayor in each of the last two local elections, yet a majority of their voters still supported Lai and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in 2024. Electing a mayor from one party hardly means a city will back that party’s presidential candidate.[...]
